transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Leah (CSM), Priya (Sundial Head Infra), Ethan (CTO), Laura (ML Eng), Owen (SRE)

Summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets, steady-state concurrency, streaming token/sec characteristics and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer is evaluating for a production rollout in H1 2027; main constraints are sub-300ms p95 for short-response assistants, larger long-form streaming for conversations, and strict data residency + KMS for some models.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency (50-500 simultaneous streams), streaming token/sec, cold starts vs warm KV cache, batching, quantization tradeoffs, networking (VPC peering), compliance (KMS/SOC2)

[00:00] Jamie Flores: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a quick intros and then jump into the latency and throughput bits. Marcus is our SE who'll run through the benchmarks and technical tradeoffs. Leah is here for onboarding/next steps.
[00:18] Priya Kapoor: thanks Jamie, quick intro from our side: i'm Priya, i run infra at Sundial, we own deployment and security. Ethan is on for product/roadmap, Laura is our ML eng lead and will share prompt sets later, and Owen is SRE and will handle network.
[00:34] Marcus Chen: great. quick agenda: 1) understand your p95 targets and token distribution, 2) talk about hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, 3) profiling plan we recommend to validate p95 and tokens/sec. sound good?
[00:48] Ethan Morales: yes. high level, our internal SLAs are 250ms p95 for assistant completions <= 80 tokens, for longer streaming flows we can tolerate up to 800ms p95 but we need steady token throughput and predictable tail behavior. Concurrency: early prod will be ~80 concurrent users doing streaming, within six months could be 400 to 500 concurrent sessions.
[01:15] Laura Kim: to add, our prompt shape is bimodal: 60% short instruction-response (30-80 tokens), 40% multi-turn streaming long-form where total tokens per session can be 1k to 5k, generation rate expected ~12-18 tokens/sec for streaming.
[01:36] Marcus Chen: good, that maps to the typical workload we see. a couple clarifying q's: when you say 250ms p95 for the short ones, is that measured from request to first token or request-to-complete?
[01:50] Ethan Morales: request-to-first-token. we care about perceived latency. complete time for longer sessions is less critical as long as streaming starts quickly and is steady.
[02:04] Owen Park: and for network, we need the control plane to be able to reach our VPC, and we may want private deployment later for some regulated data. right now we're exploring hosted for speed to market, dedicated if costs or throughput require it, and private for compliance.
[02:22] Jamie Flores: perfect. i want to be explicit: hosted is fastest to run benchmarks and get you numbers. dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolated GPU pools which helps p95 under heavy concurrency. private (VPC/on-prem) gives the controls you want for KMS and data residency but adds ops overhead and can change cold-start profiles.
[02:44] Priya Kapoor: what about tail latencies when many sessions start simultaneously — cold kv cache vs warmed? we do big marketing bursts sometimes.
[02:56] Marcus Chen: good question. cold starts depend on model size and whether your route hits an already resident model replica. with hosted we have warm pools and autoscaling; for burst scenarios we can provision burst capacity. Dedicated you can reserve capacity so warm caches stay resident and cold starts are minimized. with private, if you manage the infra you can keep large capacity warm but it becomes your ops responsibility.
[03:20] Laura Kim: how does batching affect p95 for short responses? i.e., batching improves throughput but hurts latency at low concurrency, correct?
[03:31] Marcus Chen: exactly. continuous batching helps token/sec efficiency. for p95 sub-300ms on short completions we typically suggest small max batch sizes and aggressive max-latency thresholds in the runtime so requests are prioritized for single-request paths when latency SLO is tight. We also have KV/prefix caching to reduce repeated compute for similar prompts which helps p95.
[03:56] Ethan Morales: can you quantify token/sec per GPU for our expected model class? we're planning to use a 13B open model (quantized) initially.
[04:06] Marcus Chen: ballpark: on current optimized kernels, a quantized 13B on an A100/H100-class instance with token-level optimizations and continuous batching tuned for streaming can do ~80-120 tokens/sec steady for a single stream with single-threaded decode; with concurrent streams you get aggregated throughput — so for 100 concurrent streams expect total token/sec in the multiple thousands, but p95 per stream can vary unless you pin capacity. those numbers are approximate — we'll run your exact prompts to get deterministics.
[04:38] Priya Kapoor: what about model switching and fallback logic? if you run out of capacity mid-burst, how graceful is fallback?
[04:48] Jamie Flores: we have smart routing and fallback policies: you can set routes by cost/latency/region and Redwood can fall back to a lighter model or a quantized variant automatically. that keeps service continuity but you should expect slight quality regressions if you fall back. we log these and surface them in Console so you can correlate quality regressions with capacity events.
[05:10] Owen Park: can we do a canary that routes 5% of traffic to a fallback path to measure impact?
[05:17] Leah Ortiz: absolutely, we can set up canary rollouts and A/B for a short window and collect token-level metrics and quality evals.
[05:26] Ethan Morales: on network egress, we need to minimize cross-region hops; can Redwood pin serving region to our primary cloud region?
[05:34] Marcus Chen: yes, regional routing is supported. for hosted, we offer regional endpoints; for dedicated/private you host in your chosen region or we can provision dedicated capacity in that region, subject to availability.
[05:48] Priya Kapoor: security/keys — we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs for calls. what are the options?
[05:58] Jamie Flores: for hosted we support customer-managed KMS in our private deployments or dedicated with customer-managed keys for dedicated; we also provide detailed audit logs, SSO/SAML integration and SOC2 artifacts. we'll share the security pack after this call.
[06:14] Laura Kim: curious about quantization: do you see significant p95 improvements vs non-quantized for 13B? any signal about hallucination/regression?
[06:25] Marcus Chen: quantization (4-bit/llm.int8-like flows) improves throughput and often reduces memory footprint, which can reduce cold-start time and increase cache residency. quality regressions are model-dependent — we recommend benchmarking with your eval set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload.
[06:46] Ethan Morales: let's talk about our burst scenario: marketing campaign launches give us 1k concurrent sessions for ~3 minutes, repeated twice an hour. we need graceful degradation and predictable p95. do you advise hosted with burst pool or dedicated reserve?
[07:02] Marcus Chen: for that pattern, a hybrid approach is common: reserve a baseline in Dedicated for steady-state and use hosted burst capacity or autoscaling to absorb spikes. we can set automatic fallback to smaller model variants during bursts and maintain priority routing for important routes.
[07:20] Priya Kapoor: what's the cost delta roughly between keeping baseline dedicated capacity vs paying for hosted burst traffic?
[07:27] Jamie Flores: rough math: baseline dedicated capacity has a fixed monthly cost but gives predictable unit cost at scale; paying purely hosted for bursty traffic can be higher per-token during spikes. we'll send you a cost model example scoped to your token distribution so you can compare.
[07:40] Owen Park: for the benchmarking plan, what telemetry do you need from our side?
[07:46] Marcus Chen: we'll need representative prompt sets, sample payload sizes, expected token distributions, concurrency shape (ramp-up times), region, and any egress constraints. also your success criteria for quality (ROUGE or custom evals) and p95 targets.
[08:00] Laura Kim: we'll provide three prompt sets: short assistant, medium multi-turn, and long streaming narratives. we'll also include a synthetic burst schedule to model marketing bursts.
[08:12] Marcus Chen: great. our recommended benchmark run: 1) hosted quick-run to get baseline p95/token/sec within 48 hours, 2) dedicated baseline provisioning to replicate steady-state then run concurrency sweeps up to target concurrency, 3) sustained burst test to validate KV cache warmups and cold-start behavior. total ~8-12 hours of benchmark time split across sessions.
[08:40] Ethan Morales: a couple more nitty-gritty things: what's your sess-level connection time for streaming websockets? do you support gRPC streams?
[08:50] Jamie Flores: we support streaming via HTTP chunked and gRPC streaming. session keep-alives are tunable; connection start times are mostly network-bound but at our layer we aim to push first token within your p95 targets for warmed replicas.
[09:05] Priya Kapoor: let's simulate first token latency — is it realistic to expect <250ms p95 on 13B quantized for short prompts?
[09:14] Marcus Chen: yes on warmed, pinned capacity with small batch sizes. if you rely purely on autoscaling without reserved capacity, tails can be higher during scale-up. for pinned instances we typically see p95 well under 250ms on short prompts.
[09:29] Laura Kim: we also want to evaluate token-level jitter — sometimes the stream is bursty and we need consistent tokens/sec to feed our downstream agents.
[09:38] Marcus Chen: noted. we'll collect per-token inter-arrival times and p95/p99 token-interval stats during the benchmark. that will show jitter and help you decide on buffering strategy client-side.
[09:54] Ethan Morales: any gotchas with TLS termination or mutual-TLS for private deployments?
[09:59] Jamie Flores: for private we support mutual-TLS and private endpoints. hosted supports customer-managed certs via ACM-like flows; we'll share the network/security checklist.
[10:10] Owen Park: can you summarize the best path for us to get numbers quickly?
[10:14] Marcus Chen: run a hosted quick-run with your prompt sets — we can provision that in 24-48 hours. results will include p95 first-token and completion, tokens/sec, concurrency impact, and recommendations (batch size, quant profile, route policy). based on that we can propose dedicated sizing and illustrate the cost tradeoffs.
[10:35] Ethan Morales: ok, we also want to check model fallbacks — could you run a failover simulation where primary capacity is reduced mid-run and fallback to a quantized 6B?
[10:45] Jamie Flores: yes, we can script failover scenarios and show the quality delta and latency change. we'll include that in the benchmark plan.
[10:55] Priya Kapoor: any monitoring we can plug into? we use Datadog — can we get token-level metrics and traces to Datadog?
[11:02] Marcus Chen: yes, Redwood Console emits metrics; we also offer pushing metrics to Datadog/CloudWatch via exporters and provide tracing hooks you can ingest.
[11:12] Laura Kim: what about model pinning by route? we have some customers that must always be served by a specific model version.
[11:18] Jamie Flores: supported. you can pin routes to model versions and configure rollout policies for canary or phased rollouts. that helps avoid unexpected regressions.
[11:28] Owen Park: for our SOC2-influenced teams, we probably will require private deployment for a subset of models. how different are cold starts in private vs dedicated?
[11:38] Marcus Chen: in private you control how many replicas you keep warm; if you choose to keep many warm, cold starts are similar to dedicated. the main difference is ops overhead and how quickly you can scale without manual intervention. Redwood can offer managed private deployments to reduce ops load if helpful.
[11:57] Ethan Morales: i'd like to call out one more requirement: we need 30-day audit logs retention with immutable storage for certain internal models. is that possible?
[12:06] Jamie Flores: yes, retention and immutability can be configured for enterprise tiers; we'll include that in the security doc we share.
[12:17] Priya Kapoor: what does the benchmark report look like? will you provide a CSV and dashboard snapshot?
[12:24] Marcus Chen: we'll provide raw CSVs with per-request timing, per-token traces, aggregated p50/p95/p99, token/sec plots, jitter metrics, and a Console dashboard snapshot plus recommendations and cost estimates.
[12:42] Laura Kim: thanks, that should be enough to make a go/no-go.
[12:46] Jamie Flores: quick recap/next steps: 1) Jamie sends benchmark runbook + cost sheet, 2) Laura provides prompt sets and token distributions, 3) Priya shares network diagram and SSO/KMS constraints, 4) Marcus schedules hosted quick-run (target by 2026-11-12).
[13:05] Ethan Morales: that works. any final Qs?
[13:08] Owen Park: none from me.
[13:10] Priya Kapoor: no. thank you.
[13:12] Jamie Flores: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email and Slack with the scheduling link.

End recap (explicit next steps repeated):
